etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Contraction of あの様(よう)な (ano yō na).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Early Middle Japanese adjective うまし (umashi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in き (ki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of い (i). From Old Japanese. Found in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE. Sometimes reconstructed as Proto-Japonic *uma.
The ultimate derivation remains unclear. The term occasionally appears in texts from the Heian period (794–1185 CE) with the phonetic spelling mumashi (in the classical terminal form), suggesting a possible pronunciation of */mmasi/ with an emphasized initial /mm/ sound, similar to the reconstructed readings for 馬 (*mma, “horse”) and 梅 (*mme, “plum”). The resulting reconstructed adjective stem of *mma- could indicate a derivation from onomatopoeia; compare English mmm as an expression of approval for something tasty.
Alternatively, umai is listed in some sources as perhaps deriving from verb 熟む (umu, “to ripen, to become ripe”). There is a derived compound term where the meaning is clearly from the adjective, and the spelling uses the 熟 kanji from the verb. However, the verb does not appear in historical sources with an emphatic initial /mm/, and it seems to be cognate with 膿む (umu, “to fester, to fill with pus, to produce pus”, intransitive), possibly also with 生む, 産む (umu, “to bear, to give birth to; to produce”, transitive).
Reconstructed by Samuel Martin as Proto-Japonic *ma-. Compare Okinawan cognate まーさん (māsan).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French mètre. Doublet of メーター (mētā, “meter”, measuring instrument).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨upe₂⟩ → /*upai̯/ → /upe/ → /ufe/ → /uwe/ → /ue/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *upay.
Unbound apophonic form of uwa, ancient upa (see below).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/upa/ → /ufa/ → /uwa/
From Old Japanese. The combining form of ue, ancient upe (see above).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨upe₂⟩ → ⟨pe₂⟩ → */pe/ → /fe/ → /he/ (→ /e/)
Short-form of or shift from ue, ancient upe (see above). Realized as -e in some compounds.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨kami₁⟩ → */kamʲi/ → /kami/
From Old Japanese. Already apparent in ancient texts such as the Kojiki (c. 712 CE) and the Man'yōshū (c. 759 CE).
Distinct from 神 (⟨kami₂⟩ → kami, “Shinto deity”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kami/ → /kamʉ/ → /kaɴ/
Contraction of Old Japanese ⟨kami₁⟩. Spelled in ancient works as かむ (kamu) prior to the development of the ん (n) kana.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/d͡ʑɨau/ → /d͡ʑɔː/ → /d͡ʑoː/
From Middle Chinese 上 (MC dzyangX|dzyangH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 不(ふ) (fu-, “un-; non-”) + 規(き)則(そく) (kisoku, “rule”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 何(なに) (nani, “what”) + か (ka, indefinite particle).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨pi₁kari⟩ → */pʲikari/ → /ɸikari/ → /hikari/
From Old Japanese.
Nominalization of the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 光(ひか)る (hikaru, “to shine, to glitter, to gleam”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Nominalization of the verb 光(ひか)る (hikaru, “to shine, to glitter, to gleam”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kʷau/ → /kʷɔː/ → /kɔː/ → /koː/
From Middle Chinese 光 (MC kwang).
Compare modern Mandarin 光 (guāng), Hakka 光 (kông), and Min Nan 光 (kong).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/sauzau/ → /sɔːzɔː/ → /soːzoː/
From Middle Chinese compound 創造 /创造 (t͡ʃʰɨɐŋᴴ d͡zɑu^X, literally “to begin + to make”). Compare modern Mandarin reading chuàngzào, Cantonese cong³ zou⁶.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *na (compare Okinawan 名 (nā)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 名 (MC mjieng, “name”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 回 is a daiyōji replacing 廻.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the nominalization of the verb 売(う)り切(き)れる (urikireru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 字 (“character”) + 体 (“form”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
A 国字 (kokuji, “Japanese-coined character”).
Ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 山 (“mountain”) + 上 (“up; ascend”) + 下 (“down; descend”).
Compare 裃(かみしも) (kamishimo), 垰(たお) (tao).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/tamuke/ → /taũɡe/ → /tauɡe/ → /tɔːɡe/ → /toːɡe/
Sound shift from 手向け (tamuke, “tribute to a person about to depart”). It is said that these offerings were "given" to them as they traveled into the afterlife, akin to a mountain.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Various nanori readings.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: /waupukʉ/ → /wɔːɸuku/ → /ɔːfuku/ → /oːfuku/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 忘る (wasuru), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern, from Proto-Japonic *wasuru.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/weɡaku/ > /eɡaku/
Compound of 絵 (e, “picture”) + 書く (kaku, “write”). Literally "to write a picture", ie, "to draw". The kaku changes to gaku as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 数(すう) (sū, “number”) + 学(がく) (-gaku, “-logy; -graphy”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Note similarities to Proto-Tai *tacᴰ (“to cut”) (whence Thai ตัด (dtàt, “to cut”)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: A 国字 (kokuji, “Japanese-coined character”). 木 + 卆; it is not a simplification of 木 + 卒 (椊).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 残(のこ)る (nokoru, “to remain”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The spelling is likely from Middle Chinese compound 漁師 /渔师 (ngjo srij, literally “fishing + master”). Compare modern Mandarin 漁師 /渔师 (yúshī, “fisherman”).
The expected reading would be gyoshi. The kan'yōyomi (irregular but customary reading) ryō for the character 漁 is from confusion with 猟, whose most common on reading is ryō and means hunting, as used in the homophonic term 猟(りょう)師(し) (ryōshi, “hunter”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/pakupatu/ → /bakufat͡su/ → /bakuhat͡su/
From Middle Chinese compound 爆發 /爆发 (pɑk pjot, literally “burst, explode + fly or send forth”). Compare modern Min Nan reading po̍k-hoat.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 真っ (ma'-, “truly”) + 暗 (kura, “dark”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 総理 (“prime minister”, literally “leader”) + 大臣 (“(senior) minister”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 蛍(けい)光(こう) (keikō, “fluorescent”) + 灯(とう) (tō, “light”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compare Korean 행(行) (haeng).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 議 (“debate; deliberation; discussion”) + 会 (“gathering”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 鉄(てつ) (tetsu, “iron, steel”) + 道(どう) (dō, “way”). Calque of German Eisenbahn.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 電 (den, “electric”) + 柱 (chū, “pole”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 面倒 (“inconvenience”) + 臭い (“reeks of”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Early Middle Japanese adjective 頼(たの)もし (tanomoshi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in しき (shiki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of しい (shii). Itself an adjectivization of the verb 頼(たの)む (tanomu, “to request; to entrust to”).
